tb21_profile.skill: Rewrite a SQL query into a provably output-identical but far faster form against a database you may not modify: read the query plan, remove correlated subqueries and repeated scans, restructure joins/CTEs/aggregation so the existing indexes are usable
tb21_profile.domain: SQLite, EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN and the SQLite query planner, WordNet's relational schema, SQL semantics (joins, DISTINCT, GROUP BY, ordering)
tb21_profile.task_form: optimise-for-a-budget under an exact-output-equivalence constraint, delivered as a single .sql artifact

TMax-15K.reason: Rewrite a report query that has an implicit cross-join and save the corrected SQL to its own .sql file; same rewrite-SQL-to-a-file-preserving-intended-results contract.
Replace multi-round-trip query logic with a single efficient CTE/window query; collapsing repeated scans into one pass is the core rewrite this task needs.
Read the schema, run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on the given query.sql, and act on what the planner reports. Same diagnostic loop; the fix is indexes rather than a rewrite.
An optimized pipeline must produce the exact same output array as the naive one and beat a wall-clock limit - the same-output-but-faster contract, outside SQL.
Given a SQLite schema and a slow query, make it fast; the plain form of this task with the schema delivered out of band.
Troubleshoot and optimize queries over an ETL dependency graph in SQLite, including recursive traversal; strongly verified numeric results.
Hierarchical graph analytics in SQLite where the naive recursive query is too slow; recursive-CTE cost reasoning with pinned answers.
Investigate why a query over backup_jobs is slow and fix it while keeping the reported rows identical.
Fix a broken query and then produce its EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN; forces you to read a plan rather than guess at cost.
Write an exact paginated query and dump its EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN; plan-reading practice on LIMIT/OFFSET, a classic slow pattern.

Recursive-Task-Synthesis.reason: Load data and deduplicate keeping the last occurrence per key - real SQL set semantics, the kind of clause whose rewrite must preserve exact rows.
Reorganise a table into a different schema in a live PostgreSQL instance; relational restructuring with correctness checks.
Export every table from MySQL with full contents and rebuild them in SQLite; forces you to understand a whole schema before querying it, as this task does with OEWN.
Apply tables, views, triggers and seeds in dependency order; schema-object ordering, not query performance.
Build a SQLite database from SQL files in the right order and produce a verification report; SQL execution, no optimization.
Create a table from schema.sql and load a CSV into PostgreSQL; loading rather than querying.
Resolve a UNIQUE constraint violation during initialization; constraint semantics, adjacent to index semantics.
N-Queens solver that must stay fast at larger N; search-space pruning is the same instinct as removing work from a query, different domain entirely.
Another ex1.db initialization variant; near-duplicate of the cluster, listed to fill the quota.
Create a table via SQLAlchemy and list its rows; quota filler - RTS has no query-performance content at all.

TerminalWorld-Seeds-Clean.reason: Discover every table in an unfamiliar SQLite database and extract it faithfully - the schema-reconnaissance step before you can safely rewrite a query over OEWN.
Write a three-table join against a real relational schema to pull out a specific permission set; join construction with an exact expected result.
Turn newline-delimited JSON into a SQLite database and query it; schema design plus SQLite mechanics.
Build a multi-table SQLite schema with the right keys and constraints; understanding which columns are indexed by construction is what the planner exploits.
Alter and bulk-update a large employees table in MySQL with an exactly specified transformation; set-based SQL on real data volumes.
Initialize and run a pgbench workload at a given scale; the benchmark-a-database-workload framing behind 'as efficient as possible'.
Write stream-stream left joins in KSQL; join semantics in a different engine.
Explore how primary keys are assigned via an ORM; rowid/primary-key semantics, at trivial depth.
Create a two-column SQLite table with SQLAlchemy; SQLite domain only.
Near-duplicate of the previous one; quota filler.

SWE-Smith-Seeds-Clean.reason: Fix `eliminate_joins` in sqlglot's optimizer - a rule that deletes joins that cannot change the result. Exactly the equivalence-preserving rewrite this task must perform by hand.
Subquery structure mishandled by the SQL formatter; forces precise reasoning about nested query structure, which rewriting a subquery-heavy query needs.
Pagination SQL generated wrongly for two dialects; LIMIT/OFFSET emission, the classic slow-query construct.
SQL dialect parsing regression in sqlglot; working inside a SQL AST is the same representation a rewrite operates on.
Dialect grammar breakage in a SQL linter; deep SQL syntax knowledge, no performance component.
Reindentation breaks around certain keywords; SQL statement structure at the token level.
COUNT(*) built incorrectly by the query builder; aggregate-construction correctness.
Parameterized query fails on quoted values; SQL execution plumbing, not planning.
Optimizer hints stripped along with comments - notable only because this task must emit SQL with no comments at all.
Trailing semicolons not stripped on split; trivially related to this task's 'one query terminated by a semicolon' requirement.

SWE-Rebench-Tasks-Clean.reason: A scalar subquery inside a function is missed by lineage analysis; requires tracing exactly which tables a nested query touches - the analysis a safe rewrite depends on.
Keyset (seek) pagination library broken for a column type; keyset pagination is the standard rewrite that makes an OFFSET query fast.
Second keyset-pagination bug in the same library; ordering and tie-breaking semantics that a rewrite must preserve exactly.
SQL parsing/lineage gap; reasoning about what a statement actually reads, which is how you prove two queries are equivalent.
Linting a migration that adds an index with a condition; understanding when an index is valid and useful.
Migration linting around foreign keys and related names; schema-change semantics.
A query returns only the first page instead of all results; paging correctness, a frequent source of silent output differences.
SQLite connector misconfiguration; SQLite plumbing only.
SQL-driven geospatial file operations over SQLite-backed formats; SQL generation in a niche engine.
Tabular import/export bug; filler - this corpus has nothing about query cost.

Terminal-Lego-15k.reason: Investigate when SQLite actually uses a multi-column index and when it falls back to a scan; the single most load-bearing fact for rewriting a query against fixed indexes.
Replace slow skip()-based pagination on a 300k-record collection with an equivalent fast access pattern; same rewrite-for-speed-keeping-results task, different engine.
Make a LIKE query over ~95k rows fast; forces you to understand why a predicate form defeats an index and what equivalent form does not.
Demonstrate how SQLite indexes primary keys and when an explicit index is redundant; rowid/INTEGER PRIMARY KEY behaviour the planner relies on.
Show and fix SQLite write-side degradation caused by an index; makes the cost model of indexes concrete.
Diagnose high database CPU back to the queries causing it; the measure-then-attribute step before optimizing.
Show that an implicit WHERE-join and an explicit INNER JOIN produce the same result; exactly the equivalence argument a rewrite rests on.
Group rows and concatenate a column with GROUP_CONCAT in SQLite; an aggregate whose ordering semantics matter when you restructure a query.
COUNT / GROUP BY / ORDER BY count in SQLite with a pinned result; the aggregate shape most rewrites have to preserve exactly.
Use explain on an aggregation pipeline; plan-reading habit in a non-SQL engine.

CalibForge.reason: 'A query saved in /app/slow_query.sql is not optimized. Rewrite it to be as efficient as possible producing the exact same rows, columns and order. Save to /app/sol.sql, single query, no comments.' Same task, different database.
Make four slow reporting queries fast against a 500K-row SQLite database with identical results, no data changes, using EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN; a budgeted version of the same problem.
Analytics queries against a four-table SQLite database time out; make them fast without changing what they return.
Build a columnar, vectorized, iterator-model query engine; teaches from the inside why one plan costs far less than another.
Hash join over CSV files in C; join algorithms and their cost, which is what you are choosing between when you restructure a query.
Complete the execution engine behind a SQL parser so SELECTs run correctly; SELECT semantics from the implementer's side.
Two aggregate metrics come out wrong from SQL over SQLite; fixing them demands exactly the join-fan-out and grouping reasoning that keeps a rewrite output-identical.
Write the missing executor of a SQL engine whose parser and storage layer already exist; operator semantics for joins, filters and projections.
Write non-trivial analytical SQL over a transaction database to an exact answer; query authorship against a real schema.
Read a SQLite file's raw b-tree pages in C without the library; the storage layout that decides what an index scan actually costs.

final_top10.reason: Same instruction down to the artifact: rewrite /app/slow_query.sql for speed with identical rows, columns and order, save one comment-free query to /app/sol.sql.
Four slow SQLite reporting queries over 500K rows must become fast with identical results and no data changes, using EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.
Timing-out analytics queries on a multi-table SQLite database must be made fast without changing their output.
Rewrite a query with an implicit cross-join and deliver the corrected SQL as its own file; equivalence-preserving SQL rewriting as the deliverable.
Collapse repeated query round-trips into a single CTE/window query - the main structural move available when you cannot add indexes.
Repair sqlglot's eliminate_joins optimizer rule - removing joins that provably cannot change the result, the same reasoning applied by hand here. repo-tests verified.
Read the schema, run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on the supplied slow query, and act on what the planner says; the diagnostic half, strongly verified.
Determine empirically when SQLite will and will not use a multi-column index; decides which rewrites actually help on a read-only database.
Replace slow skip-based pagination over 300K records with an equivalent fast access pattern; textbook rewrite-for-speed with unchanged results.
An optimized pipeline must emit byte-identical output to the naive one under a hard time limit - the exact-equivalence-plus-speed contract, outside SQL.

notes: CalibForge wins this one outright: data-science_20260604_003814_005 is a near-verbatim restatement of query-optimize, down to writing a single comment-free query to /app/sol.sql, and it is graded strong. optimization_20260604_003814_001 and optimization_20260606_153537_001 cover the same ground with explicit EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN guidance and identical-results constraints, and CalibForge additionally has a whole query-execution-engine cluster (columnar/vectorized engine, hash join in C, SQL executors over CSV) that teaches why a plan is fast rather than just that it is. Terminal-Lego is the surprise second: buried under a lot of trivial SQLite-syntax demos there are real ones - multi-column index usage, LIKE optimization, skip-pagination rewriting, index write-cost. TMax's SQLite cluster is large (121 EXPLAIN/index hits) and genuinely on-topic, but almost all of it solves the problem by CREATE INDEX, which this TB2.1 task forbids because the database is read-only; I ranked the rewrite-flavoured ones above the index-flavoured ones for that reason, and the merge should keep that distinction. SWE-Smith contributes one excellent item (sqlglot's eliminate_joins optimizer rule) plus a sqlparse/pypika/sqlfluff tail that is SQL-syntax rather than SQL-cost. SWE-Rebench is thin but the sqlakeyset keyset-pagination pair and the sqllineage subquery-analysis pair are honest 3s. Recursive-Task-Synthesis could not field 10 defensible candidates: its entire SQL presence is 'initialize ex1.db from these .sql files', so ranks 4-10 score 1-2. Same cross-file caveat as my other tasks: the packet `verifier` field and work/verifier_strength.json disagree on roughly a quarter of shown candidates, and I applied FREE-if-either.
